sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A newborn's stomach and kidneys are still tiny and delicate, like a brand-new engine that can only run on one special fuel. Breast milk (or iron-fortified formula, the backup fuel) is made to match exactly what a baby can handle, though breastfed babies also usually get vitamin D drops. Cow's milk and juice are too heavy for that little engine at first, so they come later.

### Question 2

Think of your daily calories as a small backpack with limited space. A nutrient-dense food is like a small item packed full of useful gear, lots of value for little space. A candy bar takes up the same space but is mostly filler. You want the most helpful stuff per pocket of space.

### Question 3

In the first weeks, a baby's spinal cord zips itself closed like a jacket. Folate is the helper that makes sure the zipper goes all the way up without gaps. Because this zipping happens super early, moms need plenty of folate even before they know a baby is on the way.

### Question 4

A baby is like a house being built super fast, workers need tons of supplies delivered constantly. Grown-ups are like a finished house that just needs upkeep. Pound for pound, the busy construction site (the baby) needs way more fuel and water to keep building.

### Question 5

Thirst is your body's alarm bell for 'drink water,' and the kidneys are the sponge that holds water in. As people get older, the alarm gets quieter and the sponge holds less. So an older person can be low on water without their body shouting about it.

### Question 6

Teenagers grow fast, taller bones, more muscle, more blood. Calcium is the material for building strong bones, and iron helps make the extra blood. So teens are like a growth factory that suddenly needs big shipments of building materials again.

### Question 7

A baby's mouth and tummy need practice and time before they can handle solid food, like you can't drive a car before your feet reach the pedals. Push food in too soon and the baby might choke or fill up on food that has less good stuff than milk. Waiting until they're ready keeps them safe and well-fed.

### Question 8

In early pregnancy the baby is tiny, like a seed, so it barely needs extra food. Later the baby grows fast into something much bigger, and mom's body adds more blood and tissue too. That's when the extra calories are really needed, so the increase comes later, not at the start.

### Question 9

Little kids grow slower than babies, so they eat less and can be picky, refusing a food one day and liking it later. The trick is to keep calmly offering good foods in small amounts, like planting seeds again and again. Forcing them or filling them with juice backfires.

### Question 10

Older bodies burn fewer calories but still need lots of vitamins, so there's less room to fit in all the good stuff, every bite has to count. Add pills that dull appetite and eating alone with no one to cook for, and it gets easy to miss out on nutrients. Several small problems stack into one big risk.

### Question 11

Making milk every day is hard work, like running a small factory that never closes. That factory needs extra fuel and lots of water to keep the milk flowing, as much as or more than growing the baby did. Some energy comes from fat saved up during pregnancy, but mom still needs to eat and drink extra.

### Question 12

Think of bone as a savings account you fill up most when you're young. The more calcium and vitamin D you 'deposit' as a kid and teen, the bigger your bone bank gets. Later in life everyone slowly withdraws bone, so starting with a fuller account keeps bones stronger for longer.
